articles.title: Leveraging the RCEP Agreement: Innovating trade promotion and expanding markets for the wood industry. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Leveraging the RCEP Agreement: Innovating trade promotion and expanding markets for the wood industry.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
RCEP - Expanding export opportunities for the wood industry.
 The RCEP agreement was signed between the 10 ASEAN countries and 5 ASEAN partners, including China, Japan, South Korea , Australia, and New Zealand, on November 15, 2020, and officially came into effect on January 1, 2022. This is the world's largest free trade agreement in terms of market size, encompassing approximately 30% of the world's population, 30% of global GDP, and 30% of global trade. Beyond its large scale, RCEP connects economies at different levels of development and includes many of the world's important raw material sources.
 Accordingly, connecting the four existing ASEAN+ FTAs within a framework of common rules of origin facilitates businesses in diversifying raw material sources, reorganizing production, and promoting the development of supply chains in the region. For the wood industry, this is a significant advantage. Vietnam is both a center for wood processing and export, and imports a considerable amount of raw materials, machinery, accessories, and supplies for production. Therefore, the ability to combine resources from multiple RCEP members can help businesses be more flexible in organizing production, while also facilitating compliance with rules of origin for each product group. 
 The RCEP agreement expands export opportunities for Vietnamese wood businesses.
 Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Secretary General of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association, noted that the RCEP Agreement establishes a relatively unified framework of rules of origin across the bloc, allowing businesses to combine raw materials, components, and production processes from multiple RCEP members while still meeting the origin requirements, depending on the specific product. This is particularly significant for the Vietnamese wood industry as businesses increasingly participate in regional supply chains.
 Within the RCEP framework, China, Japan, and South Korea continue to be large-scale markets with strong links to Vietnam's manufacturing supply chains. These markets offer significant opportunities for wood businesses, not only for exporting finished products but also for connecting with sources of raw materials, machinery, accessories, technology, and partners in the production chain. Notably, this market group boasts a diverse customer base, including segments that are not overly demanding in terms of product requirements but have a need for wood products in which Vietnam has a competitive advantage. This presents an opportunity for many businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), to gradually expand their markets and enhance their competitiveness.
 According to the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, Vietnam's exports of wood and wood products are expected to reach approximately US$17.2 billion in 2025. In the first nine months of 2026, the export value is projected to reach nearly US$13.43 billion, a 7.3% increase compared to the same period in 2025. Besides the United States , which continues to be the largest export market (accounting for 50.1% of the market share), China and Japan remain key markets for wood exports.
 However, one of the current challenges is the low utilization rate of the benefits offered by RCEP across various sectors, with some sectors still lagging behind their potential and advantages. Regarding this, according to Lawyer Nguyen Thanh Ha, Chairman of SB LAW, RCEP creates a new competitive environment, requiring businesses to restructure their production operations, supply chains, and management methods. Meanwhile, many businesses still maintain traditional business models and are not yet ready to invest in compliance management systems. This is a bottleneck that needs to be addressed if the commitments of the agreement are to be effectively exploited.
 Referring to the difficulties in exploiting and utilizing the RCEP Agreement for the wood industry, according to Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, one of the main reasons is that businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, have not managed origin of goods well from the beginning of the supply chain. By the time they start looking for Certificates of Origin (C/O) for shipment, it is often too late. " RCEP has specific product regulations at the 6-digit HS code level, and at the same time still has requirements for documentation, direct transportation, and accurate determination of the country of origin in cases where there are tariff differences ," Mr. Hoai pointed out.
 Trade promotion must target each individual market.
 To date, the RCEP market potential for export industries remains very large. Therefore, leveraging RCEP needs to be implemented simultaneously in many aspects: good origin management from the beginning of the supply chain; proactively organizing raw material sources and production stages; thoroughly researching the needs of each market; innovating product design and increasing product value; building brands; expanding e-commerce and directly connecting with distribution systems. 
 Strengthening export promotion and seizing opportunities from the RCEP Agreement for the wood industry.
 Regarding the wood industry specifically, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai emphasized the need to gradually shift from OEM (manufacturing) to ODM (design and development) and OBM (design, construction, and brand building). Vietnam cannot be solely focused on production; it must proactively design, develop products, and build brands. AI currently creates significant opportunities for businesses, including small and medium-sized enterprises, to research consumer trends, support product design, simulate interior spaces, and significantly shorten the time from idea to product.
 Furthermore, according to the General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association, in recent years, wood industry businesses have strived to find ways and directions to expand their markets. Accordingly, instead of relying solely on direct sales channels and trade fairs, businesses and associations have proactively shifted to online sales. However, in the current context of digital transformation , trade promotion also needs to adapt.
 Specifically, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai argued that trade promotion must be selective according to market, seeking distribution partners, architects, designers, retail chains, developing B2B, B2C and e-commerce; for some potential markets, showrooms, warehouses or on-site trade representatives could be considered. “ RCEP gives us markets, but RCEP doesn’t create customers automatically. To have customers, Vietnamese businesses must understand the market, design products for that specific market, and proactively approach the distribution system of that market ,” Mr. Hoai emphasized.
 According to the Plan for Market Opening and Trade Promotion in Key Markets in the late 2026 period, aiming for a 15-16% increase in goods exports in 2026, thereby supporting double-digit GDP growth, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has identified a focused approach to market opening and export promotion. This includes strengthening guidance for businesses to take advantage of incentives from EVFTA, CPTPP, UKVFTA, RCEP, and other FTAs; and simultaneously researching and expanding into new markets in West Asia, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America to diversify export markets.
 In this context, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is focusing on strengthening market- and region-specific approaches. Specifically for the Chinese market, the strategy is to implement a "regional approach," treating each locality in China as a market for promotional activities, gradually allowing products to penetrate deeper into the distribution system. Alongside this, there is a strong shift towards official exports, a push for cross-border e-commerce, and the promotion of the signing of protocols on quarantine for agricultural, forestry, and aquatic products.
 For the Japanese market, the focus is on deeply exploiting existing FTAs such as VJEPA, AJCEP, RCEP, and CPTPP, linking export promotion with technology transfer, developing high value-added products, and meeting the trends of green and sustainable consumption and the needs of an aging society. For South Korea, the focus is on opening up agricultural markets, expanding food and seafood product categories, reviving exports of sectors such as textiles, wood, coffee, and iron and steel, while simultaneously developing e-commerce and supporting industries. Meanwhile, within ASEAN, trade promotion focuses on building a unified economic space, strengthening regional supply chain connectivity, and exploiting Halal markets, especially Indonesia and Malaysia. 
| RCEP has opened the "door" to a market encompassing approximately 30% of the global population, GDP, and trade. However, for that "door" to truly translate into orders, Vietnamese businesses must shift from a mindset of "having a market" to one of "actively building a market." When trade promotion is linked to products, brands, technology, origin, and distribution systems, the potential from RCEP can be transformed into competitiveness and sustainable export growth. |

articles.title: Australia's Chalmers calls Iran war an economic disaster, says rising yields will cost billions - investingLive
articles.summary: Australia's Chalmers calls Iran war an economic disaster, says rising yields will cost billions  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers called the US war with Iran an economic disaster that is lifting global inflation and borrowing costs, said rising bond yields will add billions to debt servicing, and said he does not expect a recession at home.
Chalmers's warning on debt servicing costs puts the spotlight on the global rise in bond yields, which is now feeding directly into government budget arithmetic. That keeps fiscal supply and credit concerns on the radar for Australian government bonds ahead of the mid-year update. His focus on energy-driven inflation reinforces the case that oil is the main channel through which the Iran war reaches the Australian economy. Any prolonged disruption to Gulf supply keeps upward pressure on both prices and the RBA. The Japan visit, centred on fuel security, also highlights how energy-importing economies in Asia are coordinating their response to the oil shock.
---
Australia's treasurer says the Iran war is a disaster for the economy, with the bill arriving through petrol prices, interest rates and the cost of the nation's debt.
Summary:
- Treasurer Jim Chalmers called the US-Iran war an economic disaster, blaming it for higher global inflation and interest rates.
- He said an end to the war can't come soon enough, while declining to advise President Trump.
- After the RBA lifted rates to a 15-year high, Chalmers said budget settings are not the main driver of prices.
- A savings package is due in the mid-year budget update, but rising bond yields will add billions to debt servicing costs.
- He does not expect a recession, but said the war is weighing on global growth. He is also travelling to Japan to meet Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama.
Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers has described the US war with Iran as an economic disaster, Bloomberg (gated) reported. He blamed the conflict for driving up inflation and borrowing costs around the world and warned that it is also dragging on global growth.
Speaking on ABC television on Sunday, Chalmers said that whatever the reasons for the war, its economic impact had been disastrous for the cost of living in Australia and globally. He said the conflict was adding substantial upward pressure on inflation, which explained why interest rates were rising worldwide. Asked whether President Donald Trump should end the war, Chalmers declined to offer advice but said an end could not come soon enough. The longer it lasted, he warned, the greater the damage to the global and Australian economies.
The treasurer was also pressed on whether government spending had contributed to above-target inflation. The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted interest rates to a 15-year high, citing both conflict-driven energy costs and domestic capacity pressures. Chalmers said spending growth had slowed and that budget settings were not the main driver of prices.
He flagged that a savings package would be included in the mid-year budget update, but cautioned that rising global bond yields would add billions of dollars to the cost of servicing public debt. He said pressure on budgets in Australia and elsewhere was intensifying, and it was unclear how the savings would net out against higher borrowing costs.
Chalmers said he did not expect a recession in Australia but acknowledged the war was weighing on global growth and that the country was not immune.
He also announced plans to travel to Japan to meet Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, as well as business leaders and investors. He said the two countries faced similar pressures from higher energy prices and bond yields, and that the visit would focus on investment, fuel security and closer ties.

articles.title: After US-China tariff deal, will orders shift away from Vietnam? - Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam
articles.summary: After US-China tariff deal, will orders shift away from Vietnam?  Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

source_detail.name: Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

articles.full_text:
Speaking to Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper, Rizwan Khan, managing partner at investment consultancy Acclime Vietnam, said the latest tariff reductions cover only a limited share of bilateral trade.
Around US$60 billion worth of goods is covered by the tariff-reduction mechanism, accounting for about 14 percent of U.S.-China trade in 2025.
Of this, some $30 billion worth of Chinese goods could see lower U.S. tariffs, equivalent to 9.7 percent of China’s exports to the U.S..
The average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods would also fall only modestly, from about 22 percent to 20.5 percent, still nearly double the 11 percent level recorded in early 2025.
Short-term pressure on orders
Khan said most of the products covered are non-sensitive goods, but some categories are important to Vietnam, including toys, plastics, and household products.
These are low-margin, highly price-sensitive industries, meaning even a small tariff difference can affect sourcing decisions.
“Some U.S. buyers may shift part of their short-term orders back to existing suppliers in China, particularly for products whose tariffs return to most-favored-nation levels,” he said.
Still, Khan said the impact is more likely to emerge through order volumes and price negotiations over the next few quarters than through factory relocation.
For multinational companies, moving production is a long-term decision involving investment cycles of 10 to 20 years and substantial costs in supplier networks, logistics, and labor.
The tariff changes therefore have some significance, he said, but they are not broad enough to fundamentally alter the investment logic behind China+1, the business strategy of avoiding investing only in China or sourcing only from China.
Investors will also wait for clarity on final tariff rates, product coverage, and the duration of the reductions, as well as U.S. rules on origin and transshipment, Vietnam-U.S. trade negotiations and the tariff gap between China and alternative manufacturing bases.
Khan said China+1 remains a broader strategy aimed at reducing supply-chain concentration and geopolitical risk, rather than merely a response to tariffs.
Vietnam urged to strengthen domestic value
For Vietnam, Khan said a key priority is to conclude a reciprocal trade arrangement with the U.S. and address concerns raised by Washington, including non-tariff barriers.
Vietnam could also help ease concerns over its bilateral trade surplus by increasing purchases of U.S. products where there is genuine demand, such as agricultural goods, liquefied natural gas, and aircraft.
Rules of origin are another key issue.
As the U.S. steps up scrutiny of tariff evasion and transshipment, Vietnam will need stronger systems to verify where goods come from and how much processing takes place domestically.
Khan suggested digitizing certificates of origin, increasing oversight of projects at risk of being used mainly for transshipment, and improving supply-chain traceability, including compliance with U.S. forced-labor requirements.
He also said Vietnam needs to raise the share of value created at home.
Many manufacturing sectors still depend heavily on imported components and raw materials. In electronics, for example, industry estimates put the localization rate at only around 15-20 percent.
Building stronger domestic Tier-1 and Tier-2 supplier networks would help Vietnam retain more value and reduce its reliance on imported inputs.
“The goal should not simply be to attract another factory, but to build the capabilities of suppliers and supporting industries around that factory,” Khan said.
Beyond a manufacturing base
Human resources and energy will also become increasingly important as the next wave of China+1 investment moves into more advanced industries.
Future projects will require technical workers in semiconductor design and testing, automation and supply-chain management, as well as better access to renewable energy.
For Vietnam, Khan said the opportunity is therefore no longer just about absorbing production leaving China.
“The more important question is not whether China+1 will continue, but whether Vietnam can move from being an alternative manufacturing location to becoming an increasingly integrated and higher-value link in global supply chains,” he said.
U.S.-China tariff deal
The U.S. and China agreed in late September to reduce tariffs on about $30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods in each direction following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.
According to the White House, the agreement covers U.S. exports to China such as agricultural products, wood, and cosmetics, while Chinese exports to the U.S. include small appliances, toys, and decorations.
The two sides described the deal as a consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment, rather than a blanket tariff cut across all bilateral trade.

articles.title: Persian Gulf oil flows return to prewar levels, but Iran could resort to a 'scorched earth campaign' - Fortune
articles.summary: Persian Gulf oil flows return to prewar levels, but Iran could resort to a 'scorched earth campaign'  FortuneOil slips as Middle East crude exports rise, G7 to release stocks  ReutersIran has lost considerable leverage in the Strait of Hormuz. It can’t go on like this forever  CNNThree reasons Middle East oil supply is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels  BBCThe Return of Middle East Oil  nytimes.com
articles.full_text:
Iran is losing leverage over the Strait of Hormuz as oil exports recover under the protection of the U.S. military, but the Islamic Republic is unlikely to stand by and watch while its own economy crumbles.
This past week, JPMorgan said Middle East crude exports reached about 17.5 million barrels per day, or 98% of prewar levels. Goldman Sachs was even more bullish, estimating that exports from Persian Gulf producers hit 19 million barrels per day.
Similarly, Kpler declared Gulf crude exports have recovered to prewar levels, though it said the September number was at least 16.5 million barrels.
“The recovery has reshaped regional oil logistics,” it said on Wednesday. “Around 40% of crude now leaves without crossing Hormuz, up from 17% before the war, as Saudi Arabia and the UAE make greater use of pipeline routes. Of the crude that crossed Hormuz in August, more than 70% changed tankers offshore. The volumes have recovered, but through a fundamentally different export system.”
While crude prices remain high, with refined fuels like diesel suffering an even worse shock, the rebound in Gulf oil flows has come despite the U.S. naval blockade keeping Iran’s exports at essentially zero.
President Donald Trump and others in his administration have touted the numbers, boasting the U.S. now controls the strait and predicting Iran’s economy will soon come completely undone.
But analysts have warned the Iranian regime, facing an existential threat to its rule, could re-escalate the war and reassert its grip on the oil trade.
In fact, attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf have been on the rise in recent days. While the U.S. military is protecting ships and has degraded Iran’s ability to target them, drones and missiles still find their marks on occasion.
The attacks haven’t deterred all tankers from making the risky transit, but they keep shipping and insurance costs high, preventing the market from fully returning to normal.
Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, argued Iran’s influence over the region’s energy trade isn’t limited to the Strait of Hormuz.
He pointed out Iran can still destroy oil infrastructure, such as drilling and refining capacity—and can escalate if “Trump isn’t feeling enough pain to take the diplomatic off-ramps being put in front of him.”
Indeed, Trump has rejected Tehran’s offer to restart talks with a seven-day ceasefire that would fully reopen the strait in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade and unfreezing assets.
Rather than return to diplomacy, Trump expects to start bombing Iran again after the U.S. midterm elections are over, sources told the Wall Street Journal. Meanwhile, he is also deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, comprised of three amphibious ships and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, to the Middle East.
“So while the risk premium around oil flows may seem tolerable for Trump, the threats to energy production infrastructure in the Gulf remain significant, which is exactly why regional countries are still trying to mediate a return to a durable ceasefire and diplomatic agreement,” Batmanghelidj posted on X on Monday. “Trump too, is erratic, and could give cause to Iran to escalate in this way through his own fixation on ‘winning’ the war.”
He added that Iran’s attacks on U.S. bases in the Mideast as well as on Gulf cities and infrastructure were far more consequential as they highlighted the U.S. failure to mitigate or degrade the threat.
So while the U.S. military can keep oil flowing, it’s no longer able to guarantee security across the Gulf region, providing Iran leverage in any negotiations, Batmanghelidj said.
“Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign—but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long,” he warned. “That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.”
Of course, Iran’s own oil infrastructure would also face destruction as the U.S. and its Gulf allies retaliate.
For now, Trump has signaled he will let his economic warfare against Iran play out, and the U.S. tightened its sanctions further last month, making it harder for Tehran to move money through front companies and other shadowy intermediaries.
As Iran’s ability to generate oil revenue fades, the currency has plunged to new lows, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian complained the regime’s money in China is blocked.
“We can’t even get our own money out of a country to which we’ve supplied goods, let alone using those funds to pay someone else in another corner of the world,” he told Fox News last week.

articles.title: De-Risking and Diversifying: Jaishankar Outlines Global Strategy at Munich Security Conference - The Indian Awaaz
articles.summary: De-Risking and Diversifying: Jaishankar Outlines Global Strategy at Munich Security Conference  The Indian Awaaz
articles.full_text:
BIBHUDATTA PRADHAN
External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar has flagged international peace, supply chain resilience, and connectivity as critical anchors for Emerging and Middle Powers (EMPs). Speaking at the 62nd Munich Security Conference in New Delhi, he emphasized that these nations—spanning both the Global South and Global North—are uniting to secure greater global relevance amid a rapidly shifting geopolitical landscape.
He pointed out that the world is changing, its agenda and landscape is changing, and there is a substantial agenda for emerging and middle powers to cooperate.
Dr Jaishankar drove home the point that the changing landscape which drives the Emerging and Middle Powers debate is one of a repositioning of the US, the rise of China, and greater interdependence. He highlighted that EMPs’ approach is to de-risk and to diversify, and pursue agenda-based cooperation. He added that the resulting outcome is multipolarity, multi-alignment and small groups. He remarked that the emerging and middle powers have an interest in strengthening their interstate cooperation, but it is also natural that they would have cooperation with the US and China. He cited Quad as an example of emerging middle-power cooperation with an emerging power. He further stated that in the field of connectivity, there is the India-Middle East-Europe Connectivity Corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor, and the Northern Sea Route. Dr Jaishankar stated that BRICS is an example of various parties who feel that their collective voice is much stronger than the individual ones.
Later, in conversation with President of Munich Security Conference, Wolfgang Ischinger, and State Secretary, Germany’s Federal Foreign Office, Bernard Kotsch, Dr Jaishankar said India has decades of high growth ahead and a demography which will sustain that level of growth. He observed that India has historically tended to look at the larger nations of Europe, which is not the case anymore, and India is in the process of intensifying its relationship with the EU. He added that advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI and space capabilities are areas where India-EU partnership can increase. The External Affairs Minister also highlighted that many Indian defence start-ups have found partners abroad and defence exports are growing rapidly.

articles.title: ASEAN: A Strategic Launchpad for Malaysian Exporters - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: ASEAN: A Strategic Launchpad for Malaysian Exporters  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
ASEAN has long served as a traditional export market and strategic springboard for Malaysian businesses seeking expansion beyond the domestic market. Its geographical proximity and longstanding economic ties have created a promising avenue for trade and business collaboration to prosper.
Over the years, trade with neighbouring ASEAN countries evolved from largely border-based commerce into a robust regional trading network, as logistics and infrastructure progressively improved.
To facilitate a free flow of goods within an integrated single market in Southeast Asia, the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) was established to progressively reduce and eliminate tariffs on goods originating from ASEAN member states. As of 2025, tariffs on around 98.86% of products are fully eliminated under ATIGA.
In Malaysia’s case, integration into ASEAN has historically reinforced Malaysia’s position as a manufacturing and export hub, with more than half of the country’s exports linked to the global value chains (GVCs).
As one of the world’s fastest-growing economic regions, ASEAN continues to provide significant opportunities for Malaysian businesses to expand their footprint, particularly in high-growth sectors such as manufacturing, digital economy, services and halal industries.
ASEAN has become an ideal testing ground for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and first-time exporters to gain valuable export experience, validate their products and business models, and build confidence before venturing into more distant and competitive global markets.
As Malaysia’s national trade promotion agency, the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) plays a pivotal role in developing and promoting Malaysian exporters’ capability to become highly competitive in international markets.
Malaysia’s notable export growth was underpinned by record-high shipments to key trading partners like ASEAN. For the last decade, ASEAN has consistently remained Malaysia’s largest regional trading partner and export market, accounting for more than one-quarter of total trade annually.
Malaysia’s double-digit share of exports to ASEAN markets such as Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia underscore a strong regional integration and increasingly interconnected supply chain.
In 2025, exports to ASEAN reached the highest value ever recorded to RM458.18 billion, driven primarily by increased shipments of electrical and electronics (E&E) products, optical and scientific equipment as well as machinery, equipment and parts.
During the period of January-August 2026, Malaysia’s trade with ASEAN expanded by 25.8% to RM641.40 billion compared with the corresponding period in 2025. Exports to the region grew by 22.7% to RM368.07 billion, driven by higher exports of E&E products, petroleum products, machinery, equipment and parts, optical and scientific equipment, as well as manufactures of metal. Meanwhile, imports from ASEAN increased by 30.2% to RM273.33 billion.
Against this backdrop, strengthening intra-ASEAN trade has become increasingly important to the region's economic resilience. Greater market access and reduced trade barriers would create new opportunities for Malaysian businesses, particularly the micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to expand their regional footprint.
In 2024, intra-ASEAN trade reached USD823.1 billion, accounting for 21.4% of the region’s total trade. While tariffs within ASEAN are nearly eliminated, non-tariff barriers in the form of export restrictions and regulatory hurdles continue as major bottlenecks for many decades.
Aligning customs procedures, sanitary standards, and technical regulations across all member states will streamline the cross-border movement of goods. Expanding cross-border digital infrastructure and implementing frameworks like the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) will accelerate service and e-commerce transactions.
As ASEAN embarks on a new phase of regional integration under the ASEAN Community Vision 2045, the bloc is evolving into a more integrated, digitally connected and resilient economic community.
ASEAN is projected to become the world’s fourth-largest economy and Timor-Leste’s accession to ASEAN is expected to further strengthen regional trade integration and expand opportunities across Southeast Asia.
Amid heightened geopolitical uncertainties, including the ongoing conflict in West Asia that has disrupted logistics and supply chain challenges, ASEAN’s role as a stable and integrated regional market has become increasingly significant.
Through frameworks such as the upgraded ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA), Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), and subregional initiatives including BIMP-EAGA and IMT-GT, businesses can tap into greater market access and participate more actively in regional value chains.
MATRADE plays a pivotal role in facilitating Malaysian businesses to capitalise on ASEAN’s growth opportunities and strengthen their presence within the regional market. Through its extensive network of overseas trade offices across ASEAN, MATRADE provides market intelligence, facilitates business matching initiatives, and delivers targeted export promotion programmes, including the International Sourcing Programme (INSP), Export Acceleration Missions (EAMs), and participation in major trade fairs.
“ASEAN remains one of Malaysia's most strategic export markets and an important gateway for Malaysian companies expanding across the region and beyond. MATRADE is committed to ensuring Malaysian exporters are well-positioned to seize emerging opportunities, strengthen regional partnerships and enhance their competitiveness across Southeast Asia by helping them leverage regional frameworks such as the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) and Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).
To translate this commitment into tangible business outcomes, MATRADE continues to organise targeted export promotion initiatives across the region. These include the Export Acceleration Mission to Cambodia, participation in National Pavilion at Vietnam Expo 2026, International Healthcare Week Bangkok 2026, and ASEAN Online Sale Day 2026, which enables Malaysian businesses to reach consumers across the region through cross-border e-commerce. Through these strategic platforms, Malaysian companies can engage directly with quality buyers, establish long-term business partnerships and explore new growth opportunities, reinforcing Malaysia's position as a competitive and trusted trading nation within ASEAN,” said MATRADE Chief Executive Officer Dato’ Indera Abu Bakar Yusof.
Flagship events such as the Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) can further connect Malaysian exporters with regional and international buyers, reinforcing Malaysia’s position as a competitive trade and halal hub.
As ASEAN continues to evolve as a dynamic and integrated economic region, Malaysian companies are encouraged to leverage MATRADE’s programmes and expertise to explore new opportunities and accelerate their export journey across ASEAN.

articles.title: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel - CBS News
articles.summary: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel  CBS News‘Ready to Blow His Stack’: How Biden Nearly Cut Off Netanyahu Over Gaza  nytimes.comBiden Reportedly Considered Cutting Arms to Israel  YahooHow Biden Averted a War With Iran  The AtlanticTranscript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026  CBS News
articles.full_text:
President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.
"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."
The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."
In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
In McGurk's interview with CBS News, the longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"
Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.

articles.title: Cesar Virata: A life in the service of economic nation-building - Manila Bulletin
articles.summary: Cesar Virata: A life in the service of economic nation-building  Manila Bulletin
articles.full_text:
The passing of Cesar Enrique Aguinaldo Virata at 95 closes an important chapter in the economic history of the Philippines.
A grandnephew of Gen. Emilio Aguinaldo, the first President of the Philippine Republic, Virata carried a distinguished family name. But his own legacy was built less on lineage than on scholarship, public service, economic management, and decades of engagement with Philippine business.
His was an unusually long and varied career.
A University of the Philippines graduate who earned degrees in mechanical engineering and business administration, both with honors, Virata pursued an MBA in industrial management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. He returned to the Philippines to teach and eventually became dean of the UP College of Business Administration. During his deanship from 1960 to 1967, the MBA program was instituted at UP. His alma mater would later name its business school the Cesar E.A. Virata School of Business.
Before entering the Cabinet, Virata also gained valuable private-sector experience with SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co., where he rose to become principal of its Management Services Division.
In government, Virata became one of the country’s longest-serving economic managers. He headed the Department of Finance from 1970 to 1986. He was Prime Minister from 1981 until the transition of government in 1986. He also served as Philippine governor to the World Bank and Asian Development Bank and participated in major international economic and financial institutions.
His NEDA role deserves historical precision. Virata served as Director-General of the National Economic and Development Authority in 1983-1984, concurrently with his premiership.
Virata’s government career unfolded under Ferdinand Marcos during a period marked by both ambitious economic planning and profound political controversy. Martial Law, declared in 1972, brought centralized decision-making and restrictions on civil liberties, while the administration pursued infrastructure expansion, industrialization, and closer engagement with international lenders. These policies produced important investments and periods of growth, but they also coincided with crony capitalism, corruption allegations, rising inequality, and the concentration of economic power in politically connected hands.
The economic record became especially difficult in the early 1980s. Heavy foreign borrowing, global recession, higher interest rates, and declining investor confidence contributed to a severe debt and balance-of-payments crisis.
The assassination of opposition leader Benigno ‘Ninoy’ Aquino Jr. in 1983 further damaged political legitimacy and intensified economic uncertainty. The resulting contraction, unemployment, inflation, and social hardship exposed the limits of technocratic management when institutions were weakened and major decisions were concentrated within an authoritarian system.
While Virata was not the principal political architect of that system, he was one of its most prominent economic officials. His record must, therefore, be assessed in two dimensions: his technical competence and institutional contributions, and his association with a government whose policies and practices remain the subject of serious historical judgment.
Recognizing his expertise does not require overlooking the abuses and economic distortions of the period; acknowledging those realities does not erase the professional responsibilities he assumed in managing the country’s finances and development programs. A balanced account must hold both truths together.
After the political transition of 1986, Virata did not retreat from national economic life. He joined the private sector and became deeply associated with Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. He had served as an RCBC adviser from 1986 to 1995, became chairman and CEO from 1995 to 1998, and subsequently served as corporate vice chairman and director. RCBC said upon his death that he had been a director since 1995 and corporate vice chairman for 26 years.
His story reminds us that nation-building is not the exclusive province of politicians. Economists, educators, managers, bankers, engineers, and other professionals can leave an enduring imprint when expertise is placed at the service of institutions and country.

articles.title: India in the Global Apparel Race: Can New Delhi Catch China, Vietnam and Bangladesh? - t.co
articles.summary: India in the Global Apparel Race: Can New Delhi Catch China, Vietnam and Bangladesh?  t.co
articles.full_text:
India is seeking to transform itself into a much larger force in the global textile and apparel industry, but the country still faces a difficult competitive battle against China, Vietnam and Bangladesh, according to an analysis published by India’s World.
For more than two decades, the global apparel market has largely been shaped by China’s industrial scale, Bangladesh’s exceptionally low production costs and Vietnam’s speed and integration into international supply chains. India, despite possessing one of the world’s largest textile industries, has generally remained behind these three major competitors.
The central challenge for New Delhi is clear: India possesses enormous production capacity, a large domestic market and a vertically integrated textile sector, but it has yet to translate those advantages into a dominant position in global garment exports.
India’s textile exports reach $33 billion
India’s textile and apparel exports, including handicrafts, reached approximately $33.01 billion in FY2025-26, representing modest annual growth of around 2.1%.
When garments alone are considered, India exported roughly $16.3 billion worth of clothing in 2025, accounting for less than 4% of the global apparel market.
India’s broader share of global textile and apparel exports stands at approximately 3.9%, placing the country around sixth globally.
New Delhi, however, has much bigger ambitions.
The Indian government is targeting approximately $100 billion in textile exports by 2030, meaning the country will have to dramatically accelerate manufacturing, investment, productivity and international market access over the coming years.
China still dominates — but its apparel position is weakening
China remains by far the most powerful player in the international textile and apparel supply chain.
However, an important structural change is taking place.
According to the figures cited in the publication, China’s share of global clothing exports fell to around 29.6% in 2024, its lowest level since 2010.
At the same time, China has strengthened its position further upstream in the textile supply chain.
Its share of exports in areas such as yarn and fabrics climbed to approximately 43.3%.
This means that China may gradually be reducing its dominance in labour-intensive garment production while maintaining enormous influence over the materials, components and industrial inputs used by apparel manufacturers elsewhere in Asia.
In other words, China may be retreating from part of the “sewing floor”, but it remains deeply embedded in the supply chains of its competitors.
Vietnam emerges as an apparel powerhouse
Vietnam has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the restructuring of global apparel production.
The country has combined relatively competitive labour costs with modern manufacturing facilities, efficient logistics and an extensive network of international trade agreements.
According to the report, Vietnam overtook Bangladesh for second place in apparel exports by approximately $817 million, reversing a ranking that Bangladesh had held since 2021.
Vietnam’s rapid rise has been particularly notable because the country has become deeply integrated into Asian supply chains.
However, this integration also demonstrates China’s continuing importance.
The analysis states that approximately 44% of the foreign value added contained in Vietnam’s apparel exports originates from external sources, much of it linked to China.
India’s textile and clothing industry, by comparison, is considerably more vertically integrated, with imported value added estimated at around 21%.
Bangladesh maintains its powerful cost advantage
Bangladesh remains one of the world’s most formidable garment-exporting countries because of its extraordinarily competitive manufacturing costs.
Monthly manufacturing wages in Bangladesh are estimated at approximately $135-$140, among the lowest levels for any major apparel-producing economy.
This gives Bangladesh a substantial advantage in highly price-sensitive products such as basic garments.
The country’s economy is also considerably more dependent on garment exports than India’s.
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry represents a very large share of national exports and plays a central role in employment and economic growth.
As a result, Dhaka has built an entire industrial ecosystem focused on producing clothing for global retailers at enormous scale and low cost.
India’s labour-cost dilemma
India faces a more complicated position.
The country has a vast workforce and significant textile expertise, but manufacturers do not always enjoy the same cost advantage available to Bangladeshi producers.
At the same time, Indian apparel production often struggles with fragmented manufacturing structures, smaller factory sizes, regulatory complexity and differences in productivity across states and industrial clusters.
These factors can reduce India’s competitiveness even when nominal wages appear relatively low.
For mass-market apparel manufacturers, relatively small differences in labour costs, logistics expenses and delivery times can have a major effect on purchasing decisions.
That is one reason international brands have increasingly expanded production in Vietnam and Bangladesh rather than transferring significantly larger volumes to India.
The cotton trap
India possesses one major structural advantage: it is one of the world’s largest textile producers and has access to a substantial domestic raw-material base.
But the structure of global fashion demand is changing.
International apparel production increasingly relies on synthetic and man-made fibres, while India continues to have a comparatively strong concentration on cotton.
This creates what the report describes as a type of “cotton trap.”
India may be extremely competitive in cotton-based textiles, but global fast-fashion and sportswear markets increasingly demand polyester, technical fabrics, blended textiles and other man-made materials.
Unless India expands these segments rapidly, its traditional strength in cotton may not automatically translate into higher global garment-market share.
How the quota system changed the apparel industry
The current competition has roots stretching back decades.
Under the Multi-Fibre Arrangement introduced in 1974, major importing countries imposed quotas on textile and clothing imports.
The quota system was eventually phased out under the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing, which ended on 1 January 2005.
India had hoped the end of quotas would create enormous opportunities.
However, the country did not capture as much of the newly liberalised global market as expected.
India’s share of global textile and clothing exports reportedly declined from around 3.02% in 1994 to 2.94% in 2004, before recovering to approximately 4.53% by 2014.
Meanwhile, Vietnam and Bangladesh expanded at a considerably faster pace.
The report cites historical growth rates of approximately 10.94% for Vietnam and 7.61% for Bangladesh, illustrating how quickly both countries positioned themselves inside global clothing supply chains.
China’s lost market share did not automatically go to India
One of the biggest strategic disappointments for India has been what happened as China gradually moved away from some lower-value garment manufacturing.
Many analysts initially assumed that India would be a natural beneficiary.
Instead, much of the production appears to have migrated toward Bangladesh and Vietnam.
India’s own Economic Survey had previously highlighted this problem, noting that some of the manufacturing space vacated by China was being captured by other Asian competitors rather than India.
That remains one of the country’s fundamental industrial challenges.
India has the population, raw materials, domestic market and manufacturing base to become a global apparel giant.
But having capacity is different from converting capacity into internationally competitive export manufacturing.
Tariffs reshape the competition
Trade policy is now becoming another major factor in the global apparel race.
Changes in U.S. tariff policy have affected China, Vietnam, Bangladesh and India differently, repeatedly altering the relative attractiveness of sourcing garments from each country.
The report highlights how tariff announcements and subsequent policy changes created significant uncertainty for manufacturers during 2025 and 2026.
For international fashion companies, the calculation is no longer based simply on wages.
Companies must now consider tariffs, geopolitical risk, shipping costs, trade agreements, customs rules and supply-chain security when deciding where to manufacture clothing.
India therefore sees trade diplomacy as an essential component of its textile strategy.
India races to secure free-trade agreements
New Delhi has intensified efforts to secure wider access to international markets.
The publication points to India’s growing emphasis on free-trade agreements and economic partnerships, including arrangements involving the United Kingdom, EFTA countries and other major trading partners.
But Vietnam retains a significant structural advantage.
Vietnam is already integrated into a dense network of international trade agreements, including participation in arrangements such as CPTPP and RCEP, while also benefiting from its agreement with the European Union.
This gives Vietnamese exporters preferential access to a wide range of major markets.
India is attempting to close that gap.
Why apparel matters enormously for India
The competition is not only about export statistics.
India’s textile and apparel sector contributes roughly 2.3% of GDP and directly employs approximately 45 million people.
That makes it one of the most socially and economically important manufacturing industries in the country.
Expansion of garment manufacturing could create millions of jobs, particularly for workers entering the industrial workforce.

Australia’s property market is sliding faster than many expected. House prices fell for a sixth straight month in September, and analysts are warning the downturn could stretch deep into 2027 as higher interest rates bite.
Cotality’s Home Value Index dropped 1.1% in September, leaving national values 5.2% below the March peak. The weakness was broad. All capital cities except Darwin posted monthly falls.
Wide losses across the capitals
Brisbane recorded the sharpest monthly decline among the capitals, down 1.5%. Sydney fell 1.4% and Melbourne slipped 0.7%. Darwin was the only market to edge higher, rising 0.4%.
The pullback is not confined to a few streets or suburbs. Cotality said 97% of suburbs across the capitals recorded value declines over the past three months, a sign the downturn is spreading widely through the market.
Tim Lawless, Cotality’s research director, said the cycle was now clearly negative and expected values to keep falling into 2027 because borrowing costs remain elevated. He said a drop of 10% to 15% would be a reasonable estimate. That is a sharp turn. And a serious one.
From wealth engine to drag
The reversal matters well beyond homebuyers and sellers. Australia’s long property boom has helped lift household wealth for decades, with much of family wealth tied up in real estate rather than financial assets.
Recent analysis cited by Macro Business suggested a further slump could wipe more than A$1 trillion from Australian household net worth. The same analysis noted that Australia’s average wealth per adult ranks among the world’s highest, but that standing is heavily linked to housing values.
Average residential property values in Australia were reported at more than A$1.1 million in the June quarter of 2026, more than double the level recorded in the September quarter of 2011.
Recession risk rises
The slide is now feeding concern about the wider economy. A deep and broad housing downturn can weigh on consumer confidence, spending and construction, all of which matter for growth. South China Morning Post reported the latest slump threatens economic growth, underscoring how quickly a property correction can spill beyond the housing market.
Domain’s quarterly report also pointed to a turning point, with house prices falling in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra over the quarter. Units fell in every capital city except Darwin. In Sydney, prices dropped 3.3% over the quarter, while Melbourne fell 3.1%.
Markets are watching for what comes next. If higher rates keep squeezing borrowing power and tax settings continue to cool demand, the coming months could bring another leg down. The test now is whether Australia’s housing slide stays orderly — or starts to bite harder across the broader economy.

articles.summary: Huawei to expand LogicFolding chips as it targets overseas smartphone market  Nepali Patro

Huawei plans to use its new LogicFolding semiconductor technology in more smartphones as the Chinese technology giant works to strengthen its chip capabilities and gradually expand its presence in overseas markets, Richard Yu, Huawei’s consumer business chief, said.
Yu, who joined Huawei in 1993, said the company has invested more than 1.
8 trillion yuan ($260 billion) in research and development between 2007 and 2025.
Annual R&D spending has risen from about 10% of revenue in the early years to more than 20% in recent years.
The investment has focused on core information and communications technologies and basic research, helping Huawei build its own technologies, intellectual property and patent portfolio.
Huawei’s newly launched Mate 90 series uses the Kirin 9050 Pro chip, which the company says delivers 31% higher overall performance than its predecessor.
The chip’s Balong modem, image signal processor, mobile security processor, Lingxi CPU, Maleoon GPU and NPU based on Huawei’s Da Vinci architecture were all designed by Huawei.
The Kirin 9050 Pro also incorporates Huawei’s LogicFolding technology, developed under what the company calls the Tau Scaling Law.
The technology vertically stacks logic layers and uses high-density connections between layers to shorten critical paths and reduce latency.
Huawei says the technology gives the chip strong AI processing capabilities, allowing the Mate 90 series to run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model directly on the device.
Asked whether LogicFolding chips would be used in more smartphones, Yu said Huawei had already introduced the technology in the Mate XT 2 tri-fold smartphone and that “more of our phones will definitely use these LogicFolding chips in the future.
” Yu acknowledged that China’s advanced semiconductor production capacity remains constrained by rapidly growing demand.
Huawei’s Ascend AI chips also rely on the same advanced production capacity, but the company has developed an internal requirements plan covering both AI and smartphone chips.
He said current capacity is generally sufficient for Huawei’s shipment needs, although rising memory prices over the past two years have affected smartphone sales volumes.
Huawei hopes China’s semiconductor industry will expand production capacity to support more advanced products for both domestic and international markets.
Huawei has also developed its own operating system, HarmonyOS, after beginning its development in 2019.
More than 90 million smartphones, PCs and tablets currently run HarmonyOS 6 and HarmonyOS 7, with the number expected to reach 100 million by the end of the year.
The ecosystem has more than 450,000 apps and services, 11 million registered developers and more than 23,000 app innovation partners.
Yu said Huawei is considering gradually bringing HarmonyOS to global markets.
The company, whose smartphone business was once the world’s largest, now sells only several million smartphones outside China annually but is seeking to rebuild its overseas presence step by step.
Huawei has maintained stronger positions in other product categories, including wearables, where Yu said it ranks first globally and in China.
Its TWS earphones have also reached leading positions in several countries, while HarmonyOS-based tablets and mobile routers are gaining traction in overseas markets.
Yu said Huawei had reduced its dependence on U.
S.
technologies since 2019 by developing its own operating system, software tools and domestic supply chain.
Huawei resumed domestic smartphone chip production in 2023 and now relies largely on China’s semiconductor, materials and manufacturing ecosystem.

What happened at sea
Britain's maritime alert service, the UKMTO, logged two weekend incidents involving tankers near Oman and Iran. On Saturday, it received a report that an unknown projectile hit a crude oil tanker four nautical miles east of Oman. On Sunday, another tanker was reported struck inside the Strait of Hormuz, with damage to its engine room.
Attacks in the strait have become a near-weekly feature. Before the U.S. and Israel-led war began on Feb. 28, roughly one fifth of the world's oil moved through this chokepoint.
Tehran's terms and the fragile truce
On Sunday, Iran reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed unless its conditions linked to concluding the conflict with the U.S. are fulfilled. Nour News, a state outlet, quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf saying, "The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials."
In June, President Donald Trump together with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian approved a temporary agreement, the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, briefly halting the fighting. To reopen transit, Tehran demands a stop to U.S. "acts of aggression," the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade imposed on its ports, an end to broader economic warfare, and the return of Iranian assets. The U.S. has insisted that Iran take apart its nuclear weapons program as a principal condition.
Attacks on tankers move oil prices within hours and fuel costs within weeks. Market Briefs tracks the energy market free every morning.
Saudi strike claims and a widening battlefield
The conflict's spillover is not limited to shipping lanes. Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they targeted a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, saying it was retaliation for Saudi strikes on Sanaa and other provinces. A witness told Reuters that a towering column of flames and smoke rose above the facility.
On October 3, 2026, fire was seen at an Aramco site located south of Riyadh. Saudi authorities have offered no public statement on the reported attack, and Aramco did not immediately reply to CNBC's email seeking comment. If confirmed, the episode would mark another escalation, effectively creating an additional theater in the Iran conflict.
Markets are already reacting
Some investors are bracing for a sharper downturn in the security picture. "The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," said Bader Al-Saif, the founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, speaking to CNBC's Access Middle East on Friday.
Ongoing attacks, plus the risk of further escalation, have pushed energy prices higher in recent weeks, lifting global inflation expectations and nudging government borrowing costs up. On Thursday, crude moved higher after reports that the U.S. would send to the Middle East a third strike group built around an aircraft carrier, along with an amphibious force of 2,000 Marines. Prices eased Friday after the Group of Seven said it would release diesel and crude stocks to help consumers. Brent futures slipped 6 cents to close at $102.25 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell $1.76 to settle at $91.11.
How this matters for your portfolio
Maritime hits in a corridor that once carried about a fifth of global oil can show up quickly in gas prices, inflation, and interest rates. That combo affects everything from commuting costs to mortgage math. Keep an eye on security headlines around the Strait of Hormuz and how energy and rate sensitivity show up in your own budget.

articles.title: Alex Matrsson: “Made in GCC” Is a Significant Step Towards a More Integrated, Competitive, and Future-Ready GCC Industrial Economy - dknews.kz

articles.full_text:
In an exclusive Senior Advisor interview, Mr. Alex Matrsson, the Swedish Pracademic and International Business Strategist, regards Made in GCC 2026 as a significant step in the Gulf’s industrial development because it brings policymakers, industry leaders, investors and technology stakeholders into a common environment where strategy can translate into commercial opportunity. The inaugural Forum and Exhibition will take place from 6 to 8 October 2026 at Exhibition World Bahrain in Sakhir, under the patronage of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, with the blessing of Their Majesties and Highnesses, the Leaders of the GCC member states. Mr. Matrsson sees the initiative as a practical expression of the GCC ambition to build a more integrated, competitive and future-ready industrial economy.
A Regional Industrial Vision Takes Shape
The institutional architecture matters greatly in Mr. Matrsson’s assessment. The Ministry of Industry and Commerce of the Kingdom of Bahrain has joined with the General Secretariat of the Gulf Cooperation Council to create a setting where industrial policy can meet investment, production and market development. Mr. Matrsson also points to the Forum’s timing alongside the GCC Industrial Cooperation Committee and the GCC Commercial Cooperation Committee meetings, chaired by the Kingdom of Bahrain under the leadership of H.E. Abdulla bin Adel Fakhro, Minister of Industry and Commerce. With H.E. Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Secretary General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, participating in the wider gathering, Mr. Matrsson sees a direct connection between the Forum and the region’s economic cooperation agenda.
The Economic Weight Behind the Opportunity
The scale of the surrounding economy gives Mr. Matrsson a clear basis for assessing the industrial opportunity. Made in GCC 2026 records 21,969 total firms, 426.07 billion in total investment, 1,768,344 in total labour, a population of 63.39 million, 807.96 billion in imports, 423.93 billion in exports, a trade balance of -384.03 billion and total GDP of 2,323.58 billion. With manufacturing identified as the second-largest contributor to GCC GDP after mining and oil, Mr. Matrsson regards industrial development as a central force within the Gulf’s economic diversification.
The breadth of the production base further shapes Mr. Matrsson’s assessment. Aluminium, petrochemicals and polymers, steel and metals, fertilizers and ammonia, cement and building materials, cables and wires, dairy and food, automotive, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, machinery and equipment, plastics and packaging, electronics and technology, plus logistics and supply chains form a broad industrial ecosystem. He sees the greatest strategic value in connecting these capabilities so regional production can capture more value through stronger supply relationships and deeper market access.
What Will Define the Next Industrial Cycle
For Mr. Matrsson, industrial competitiveness now depends heavily on the systems surrounding production. Global market access requires resilient supply chains, while green manufacturing, smart production, industrial financing, workforce development and infrastructure determine how effectively companies can scale. He therefore regards the Forum’s strategic priorities as a coherent response to the demands facing modern industrial economies.
Technology sits at the centre of that transition in Mr. Matrsson’s view. Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, automation and digitalisation can transform productivity, factory performance and supply-chain responsiveness when businesses integrate them into their operating models. He also connects sustainability directly with commercial performance, as environmental expectations increasingly influence investment decisions, procurement requirements and access to international markets.
Turning Capability Into Commercial Value
The exhibition gives Mr. Matrsson a practical measure of how industrial ambition can translate into business activity. GCC-made products, advanced technologies, industrial solutions and innovation will meet investors, buyers and strategic partners through dedicated investment platforms and business-to-business engagement. He sees the strongest outcome emerging when those encounters develop into investment, exports, distribution, technology cooperation or longer-term supply relationships.
Knowledge exchange adds another dimension to that process. Mr. Matrsson values the sharing of industrial best practices because companies can learn from operating experience while investors and policymakers gain a clearer view of commercial realities. Public-private partnerships can then help turn those insights into practical industrial initiatives.
The Technology and Talent Equation
The transformation Mr. Matrsson anticipates extends beyond machinery and digital systems. Artificial intelligence, automation, digitalisation and smart manufacturing can raise productivity and support higher-value production, yet their impact depends on the organisational capability surrounding them. articles.title: Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in a hemp law. Now $28 billion THC industry fights to survive - Fortune
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in a hemp law. Now $28 billion THC industry fights to survive  FortuneA $28 billion hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban  PBSYear-end countdown: The federal ban threatening to upend the THC drink boom  NPRFederal Changes Will Put Hemp Industry Operators Out Of Business, Oregon Retailers And Suppliers Say  Marijuana MomentThe Existential Threat Facing THC Drinks Brands  dail...
articles.full_text:
In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company’s signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana.
It’s a business he might soon have to give up. America’s multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers, and different from the regulated legal marijuana industry — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish.
Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the “hemp THC ban” from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them.
“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”
Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed
Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.
To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.
But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.
Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.
The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.
Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.
McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.
The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.
An industry tries to save itself
The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.
The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.
The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.
“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.
They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.
The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.
Some consider other work
Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what’s available in states that have.
“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”
That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.
Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin’ Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.
“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I’m actively looking for employment.”
Allies and opponents line up
Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.
Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.
“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.
The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.
While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It’s possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.
“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”

articles.title: Rejoining the EU would throttle Britain’s AI industry - unherd.com
articles.summary: Rejoining the EU would throttle Britain’s AI industry  unherd.com
articles.full_text:
In the first half of 2026, UK AI companies raised €12.6 billion, which is more than the rest of the European Union combined. If the UK were to re-enter the EU, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week, it would join a regulatory regime that makes a large part of those investments obsolete.
AI was one of the rare Brexit success stories, precisely because the UK chose regulatory divergence. After Brexit, the EU embarked on a frenzy of tech regulation: on AI, crypto, digital services and digital markets. The UK pursued a softer regulatory approach in all of these sectors, especially AI. On re-entry, the country would have to accept the EU’s AI regulation lock, stock and barrel, in what is known as the acquis communautaire. This is not a negotiation between UK regulation and that of Brussels. There may be transitional periods, but any new entrant has to adopt the entirety of the EU regulatory framework.
Continental Europe’s AI ventures have been mostly disappointing. Companies such as Germany’s Aleph Alpha and France’s Mistral started out with the ambition to produce frontier models and challenge global market leaders. Both are still around, albeit with reduced ambitions. They are now focused on implementation, with Mistral the more successful of the two, having raised some $3 billion in a funding round earlier this month. Still, this pales in comparison to the US, whose AI industry has invested over $500 billion so far this year.
The European commentariat has been insisting for some time now that the global AI investment boom will hit a wall, in doing so underestimating the technology’s economic significance and overestimating its dangers. These journalists share a lack of interest in a capital markets union as a precondition for making large AI investments possible. If AI succeeds, Europe will not partake fully.
In a parallel universe, there might be a situation where the EU, under more strategic leadership, would regard a Brexit reversal as an opportunity to accomplish two tasks at once. These would involve building an EU-wide capital market on top of the UK’s financial sector, and piggy-backing on Britain’s more successful regulatory regime for AI, quietly dropping its own AI Act in the process.
This is unlikely to happen, with a more probable outcome being that AI emerges as an unexpected obstacle during re-entry negotiations, as tech companies warn the UK Government that their investments are at risk in a more restrictive regulatory environment. Britain, in turn, would be shocked to find out that the EU is not ready to accept its regulatory regime as the more successful one.
If the issue of Britain rejoining the EU came up today, Rejoiners would no doubt argue that the benefits of the single market outweigh the costs of losing an edge in AI. A snapshot of current economic activity might go some way towards vindicating this assessment. But in three or four years’ time, the situation will be quite different. In any case, it is never a good idea to base economic judgments on snapshots. The dynamic interactions are far more important.
This story ties in with speculation around a coming financial crisis. The rise in US bond yields this week reflects worries about future inflation and interest rates. What weighs against this negative sentiment is the hope of a positive productivity shock due to AI. An EU that does not invest in AI will not benefit from higher productivity, but will suffer the consequences of a global sovereign debt crisis. One need only remember how the global financial crisis, which had its origins in the US mortgage market, ended up almost killing the EU’s monetary union. Static Rejoiner thinking could have very serious consequences indeed.
